headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: shared filesystem/MCP plus broad shell and git writes make the pair unsafe by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b explicitly shares state via filesystem and can read/write the filesystem. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where one agent’s outputs can be re-ingested by the other as instructions. The pair lacks provenance controls in both profiles, so the interaction is not blocked by default.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions or prompts into shared files that agent_b later reads, injection is possible.
IF agent_b treats file contents as authoritative without provenance checks, attacker-controlled text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories.
Disable automatic parsing of shared files as prompts.
Add a provenance header check before any file is treated as instructions.
Use a manual review step for inter-agent handoffs.
requires-engineering: add content-signing or allowlist-based message passing.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches task prompts, repository metadata, and secrets (Ed25519 signatures), and agent_b has read/write filesystem plus broad network egress. Because agent_b shares state via filesystem and can transmit data outward, sensitive material from agent_a can leak through shared files or copied context. The profiles do not show isolation or redaction by default.
conditions: IF agent_a stores prompts, metadata, or signatures in a shared workspace, agent_b can read them.
IF agent_b forwards file contents to configured model providers or MCP servers, those contents can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Put each agent in a separate workspace.
Remove secrets from any shared directory.
Restrict agent_b network egress to a test endpoint.
Disable automatic syncing of shared files.
requires-engineering: add per-agent secret redaction before handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. agent_b also has filesystem write and shared filesystem state, while agent_a can run background analysis tasks. Concurrent writes to the same repo or working tree can corrupt git state or overwrite each other without locking, which is dangerous in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state without a lock, history corruption or lost work is possible.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate clones.
Serialize git operations with a lock file.
Assign non-overlapping file ownership.
Disable concurrent package installs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion for shared repos.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis and task outputs, and agent_b can consume filesystem content and act with shell/git privileges. That makes it plausible for agent_b to treat agent_a’s output as authoritative and propagate mistakes into code or repo state. The profiles do not show a verification gate, but the blast radius is bounded to work products rather than guaranteed external harm.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-produced files without validation, errors can cascade into commits or shell actions.
IF agent_a emits incorrect facts or commands, agent_b may operationalize them.
mitigations: Require human review before commits.
Add checksum or schema validation on handoff files.
Mark agent_a outputs as untrusted by default.
Limit agent_b to read-only mode during review.
requires-engineering: implement a verifier agent between them.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts and repository metadata, while agent_b handles source code and files in cwd with broad filesystem access. The profiles show different retention and isolation postures, but no explicit residency or retention guarantees. That creates a compliance mismatch risk for shared regulated data, though the evidence does not show a specific regulated class like PHI or EU PII.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, the agents may retain or expose it differently.
IF retention or deletion obligations apply, the profiles do not show aligned controls.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Document a single retention policy for both agents.
Delete temporary files after each run.
Restrict logs to non-sensitive metadata.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention enforcement.
